title: An old man hears a hymn
hookLine: past sixty, Amar Das hears Guru Angad's daughter Bibi Amro singing Nanak's words at dawn, and goes to find the Guru

lines: A SONG FROM AN OPEN WINDOW.
AMAR DAS, PAST SIXTY, STILL LOOKING.
cards: A song drifts out of an open window, and a passerby stops walking. He didn't choose it; it found him. This passerby has been looking his whole life.
His name is Amar Das. Tradition says he's past sixty, a respected man in his village, deeply devout, and that he has walked to the Ganges on pilgrimage again and again.
He's done everything a devout man is supposed to do, and he still feels something missing. His nephew has married a young woman named Bibi Amro, who happens to be Guru Angad's daughter.
And one morning before dawn, Amar Das hears her singing while she works.

teach.b: She was singing a hymn of Guru Nanak's. Tradition doesn't agree on exactly which one, but the effect is the same in every telling. Amar Das stood still and listened, then asked her: whose words are those?
My father's teacher, she said, Guru Nanak. And my father, Guru Angad, carries his light now, at Khadur.

teach.h: AN OLD MAN BOWS TO A YOUNGER TEACHER.
teach.b: So an old man of standing got up and went to find a teacher much younger than himself. He bowed at Guru Angad's feet, and stayed. He would become the third Guru, but not for many years.
Notice three things. First, who carried the hymn: not a priest or a scholar, but a young woman singing while she did her morning work.

The word traveled the way it was meant to, through ordinary people's voices, in their own language. That's what Guru Angad's letters and Mardana's rebab were for. Second, what the hymns are on this path.

teach.h: BANI — THE WORD AS A LIVING TEACHER.
teach.b: Sikhs call the Gurus' words bani, and they treat bani itself as a teacher, as alive. A hymn heard at the right moment can change a whole life. Third, age.
Amar Das had every reason to think his path was settled. He'd done the pilgrimages. He was old.
Instead he started again as a beginner, and spent long years learning to serve before anyone called him Guru.
Sikhs tell his story to say the door is open at any age, and it's never too late to hear something new.

how: Sikhs honor Guru Amar Das as the third Guru and tell of Bibi Amro's singing as the moment that brought him to Guru Angad; Sikh daily practice begins with the Gurus' hymns in the early morning.

o: a pilgrimage to bathe in the Ganges
the Gurus' words, the hymns themselves
a morning chore done before dawn

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the Guru's word, a living teacher
the younger teacher he bowed to

s: Amar Das became Guru as a young man
he was already past sixty when he came to Khadur, and became Guru years later.
the hymn reached him through a young woman singing
Bibi Amro, singing Guru Nanak's hymn at dawn.
Amar Das had never been on pilgrimage
tradition says he went to the Ganges again and again.

games.q: you're past sixty and respected, and you've done every pilgrimage. at dawn you hear a hymn that stops you cold. what do you do?
o: enjoy it and go on with your day.
find out whose words they are, and go to that teacher.
decide you're too old to change paths.
games.why: Amar Das asked Bibi Amro whose words they were, and went to Khadur to bow before a Guru much younger than himself.

practice: Pick one song, maybe one you haven't heard in years, or one someone you love used to sing, and close your eyes if you can. Listen to the words as if for the first time, like an old man stopped outside a window at dawn.
Is there one line in it you never really heard before?

wordCard.voice: Bani. The Gurus' hymns, treated by Sikhs as a living teacher, one of which stopped Amar Das, past sixty, as Bibi Amro sang it at dawn.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bani, the word; for Sikhs, the Gurus' hymns, treated as a living teacher.
